article_sentences: Mahindra & Mahindra on Friday expanded its Battery-as-a-Service (BAAS) financing programme across its Electric Origin SUV lineup, moving a flat ₹8 lakh out of the upfront vehicle price of each model—the largest absolute reduction in advertised entry price among major Indian EV makers using such schemes.
The move drops Mahindra’s electric SUVs, otherwise priced from ₹19.45 lakh to ₹21.90 lakh, into an advertised bracket of ₹11.45 lakh to ₹13.90 lakh before battery financing.
In doing so, Mahindra is pushing 59-79 kWh electric SUVs into the consideration set of buyers who might otherwise begin their search with a ₹12-15 lakh petrol, diesel or CNG vehicle.
That reshuffles an increasingly important battle over advertised prices among EV makers.
Mahindra’s BE 6 SPORTEQ now starts at ₹11.45 lakh under BaaS, while the Tata Curvv.ev starts at ₹12.49 lakh after battery financing moves roughly ₹2.3-4.5 lakh out of the upfront price.
JSW MG Motor India’s Hector Tomahawk EV enters at ₹13.99 lakh under BaaS, representing an upfront shift of about ₹2.64-5.5 lakh depending on the variant.
The significance is less about which EV has the lowest headline price than where these vehicles now appear in a consumer’s shopping journey.
Car buyers typically begin with a budget rather than a powertrain.

A buyer searching below ₹15 lakh can now encounter mid-size electric SUVs offering claimed test-cycle ranges of 521 km on the XEV 9S, 542 km on the XEV 9e and 557 km on the BE 6 SPORTEQ alongside upper variants of smaller petrol and diesel SUVs.
While Mahindra’s headline entry prices apply to the 59-kWh variants, its BaaS programme also extends to the larger 70-kWh and 79-kWh battery packs.
That puts battery capacities once associated with substantially more expensive EVs within the initial price filter of a mass-market SUV shopper.
The lower entry price, however, is not a discount.

article_sentences: Congress president and Leader of Opposition in the Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, urging the government to provide humanitarian and relief assistance to flood-ravaged Nepal and intensify efforts to ensure the safety and evacuation of Indian nationals stranded there.

In his letter, dated August 28 but released on Saturday (August 29, 2026), Mr. Kharge said he was deeply concerned about the devastation caused by the floods, which, according to recent media reports, had claimed more than 600 lives and left thousands of people missing.
Thousands of people were in urgent need of food, medicines, shelter and other essential assistance, he said.

“I request you to ensure that adequate humanitarian and relief assistance is provided to the affected people of Nepal in coordination with the Government of Nepal,” Mr. Kharge urged the Prime Minister.

He also raised concerns about Indian nationals and persons of Indian origin stranded in different parts of Nepal because of the floods, urging the Centre to issue necessary directions to intensify rescue and evacuation efforts and make arrangements for their safe and early return to India.

Referring to information from the Ministry of External Affairs, Mr. Kharge said around 320 Indian nationals remained uncontactable in Nepal and called for immediate steps to provide all possible assistance.

In a separate letter to Union Home Minister Amit Shah, Mr. Kharge urged the government to consider extending “immediate and comprehensive” humanitarian and disaster-relief assistance to Nepal, underlining the deep and enduring ties between the two countries.

He said the deployment of National Disaster Response Force teams, wherever required and in coordination with the Nepal government, should also be considered to assist in rescue, evacuation and relief operations.

The NDRF’s expertise and experience in responding to natural disasters could provide valuable support in saving lives and bringing urgent relief to affected communities, Mr. Kharge said, urging the Home Ministry to treat the matter with “urgency and sensitivity”.

stories.headline: Nepal flood: 616 bodies recovered as death toll continues to rise, 2301 people injured, rescued
stories.title: Nepal flood: 616 bodies recovered as death toll continues to rise, 2301 people injured, rescued
stories.summary: Kathmandu , August 29 : Authorities have recovered 616 bodies as the death toll of the August 26 flash flood in Rasuwa district of Nepal continues to rise, while 2301 people were injured and rescued, Nepal Police said. As the flash flood hit the Bhotekoshi river system on August 26, Chitwan district witnessed the highest death toll of 233, followed by 158 in Nawalparasi (East), 48 in Gorkha, 47 in Nawalparasi (West), 45 in Dhading, 41 in Nuwakot, 31 in Tanahun and 13 in Rasuwa. According to Nepal Police, 1,422 people were rescued from Nuwakot, 676 from Rasuwa and three from Dhading. A total of 4,811 police personnel have been deployed for rescue and relief in flood-hit areas of Nepal. The Himalayan nation only has the capacity to store about 350 bodies in morgues nationwide, which has led to a shortage of space to store the bodies until the families identify and claim them. The district of Chitwan has already been filled with the bodies of victims swept downstream, which has prompted authorities to set up temporary facilities. Along with this, hospitals in Pokhara have also reported that their morgues are filling up after bodies began arriving from several districts. "All of the bodies are being recovered from the river by deploying the police team. We first retrieve the bodies from the river, take close-up photos of the bodies; if the body is not clear, then we first clean the bodies and then keep them in the body bag, tag it and bring it to this temporary body management location. Here, we maintain the room temperature at zero degrees in the AC. We have been doing it because there is a problem in identifying the bodies of the victims. If some of the relatives of the missing persons come to inquire, then we display the photos of the recovered bodies. If they identify the bodies of their missing relatives, then we will hand them over after completing the procedures," Rameshwor Paudel, Superintendent of Nepal Police, told ANI. Rescue operations in Nepal's Trishuli region have been temporarily suspended as heavy rain intensified, raising the river level and forcing authorities to halt helicopter operations due to adverse weather conditions. The worsening weather conditions have also prompted authorities to evacuate people from areas surrounding the rising river as a precautionary measure, officials said. Meanwhile, Nepal Police said that the road section between Kathmandu and Mugling is fully operational, with only a one-kilometre stretch at Baireni Bazar in Dhading operating under one-way traffic.

stories.headline: China suspends rescue operations near Nepal-Tibet border over fears of another flood
stories.title: China suspends rescue operations near Nepal-Tibet border over fears of another flood
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 28: Chinese authorities have suspended rescue operations near the Nepal-Tibet border after a lake formed by debris from a landslide began filling with water, raising fears that it could burst its banks and trigger another flood, the BBC reported. Officials have been monitoring rising water upstream from Gyirong port, a key land crossing between Nepal and Tibet that was swept away by a torrent of mud and water following Wednesday’s landslide. According to the BBC, hours of heavy rain have increased concerns that the newly formed lake could breach the debris blocking it and cause further flooding in the coming days. Rescuers in the area have reportedly been ordered to halt operations temporarily, citing reports in Chinese state media. More than 550 people have been reported missing on the Tibetan side, including around 260 foreigners. Many of those affected were pilgrims travelling towards Mount Kailash, a major Hindu and Buddhist pilgrimage site in Tibet. The latest disaster has caused heavy casualties on both sides of the border. At least 469 people have died in Nepal, with hundreds still missing, more than 48 hours after flash floods devastated the Himalayan border region. In Tibet, three people have been confirmed dead and more than 550 are missing, although it remains unclear whether some of the figures overlap. The disaster has disrupted an area visited by tens of thousands of tourists and pilgrims every year.

stories.summary: Mendhar, Aug 29: A drone suspected to be from Pakistan was spotted hovering over forward areas along the Line of Control (LoC) in Jammu and Kashmir's Poonch district, prompting security forces to launch a search operation in the area early Saturday, officials said. The drone was noticed at Balakote area’s Behrooti village in Mendhar sector late Friday evening, and it moved towards the Mangalnar-Dabrote side near the border before returning to Pakistan, the officials said. In Rajouri, another search operation was launched in Gaibas, Mithiyani, Mogla and Narla after villagers informed about the movement of two suspected armed persons, believed to be terrorists. Officials said there have been no contact with any suspected persons so far.

stories.headline: The warning Kishtwar already documents
stories.title: The warning Kishtwar already documents
stories.summary: Sometime on a Wednesday morning this month, a wall of water came down the Bhotekoshi on the Nepal-China border. It began with a magnitude 4.4 tremor about a hundred kilometres north of Kathmandu. Minutes later, researchers believe, an ice avalanche broke loose in the Lhende Khola and pushed a surge into Rasuwa and Nuwakot. By the time the water reached the plains it had taken out hydropower stations and buried villages, and a mudslide in Gyirong county on the Tibetan side added to the count. Officials in both countries have confirmed at least 98 dead ( at the time of writing this column), with hundreds missing. Early Indian reports suggested more than a hundred Indian nationals were on the Kailash pilgrim route that runs through the same valley. The detail that should trouble Indian planners is not the death toll. It is that the same stretch of river did this in July 2025, when a supraglacial lake drained upstream in Tibet and killed nine people. Fourteen months, twice. The mountain gave the same warning on two occasions, and on both it was filed as an isolated tragedy rather than read as a pattern. I have been thinking about that pattern because of a document produced by the District Disaster Management Authority in Kishtwar: its Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Risk Management Plan for 2024-25. It is a serious piece of work by the district’s own officials, and it is unusually candid. It is also, read closely, an inventory of everything that has not yet been built. Kishtwar is known to most Indians for its mountain scenery and, increasingly, for its dams. Very few know that it holds the largest concentration of glacial lakes anywhere in Jammu and Kashmir. By the DDMA’s own assessment, the district contains 197 glacial lakes, 36.08 per cent of every glacial lake in the Union Territory, spread over roughly 392 hectares in the upper Chenab basin. Most are small. About 91 per cent are under five hectares. The risk sits with the exceptions, the ones still growing as the glaciers behind them retreat. The plan singles out four. Mundiksar and Hangu are classified High Risk. An unnamed lake near 33.94°N, 76.02°E, and Patla Pani are classified Moderate Risk. These are not activist estimates. They were compiled by the district administration with the UT’s disaster management department and cross-checked against the seventeen-parameter scoring framework the Central Water Commission finalised in October 2024, which weighs lake size, dam type, seismic exposure, freeboard and distance to habitation. Mundiksar is the one worth sitting with. At about 4,071 metres and 39.44 hectares, it has expanded visibly over four decades as its parent glacier has pulled back, a change the plan’s own satellite comparisons from 1980 to 2020 document in detail. It is on the National Disaster Management Authority’s lake registry. And yet, by the plan’s own expedition record, current as of November 2024, no field survey report had been received for any of Kishtwar’s three most concerning lakes. stories.title: Israeli strikes kill 5 in Gaza, Iran touts Russian energy deal, and other news in Middle East
stories.summary: Dubai, Aug 28: Israeli airstrikes in Gaza killed five people on Friday, despite a fragile ceasefire brokered by the United States. Meanwhile, thousands of sailors remain stranded in the Persian Gulf by the Iran war, while Iran is touting an energy deal with Russia and the US has imposed restrictions on a major Egyptian bank for its ties with Iran. Here's a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here. Israeli strikes in Gaza kill 5 Israeli strikes in Gaza have killed five people, local hospital officials said Friday. Two brothers and another relative died in a strike on the family's home outside Khan Younis, officials at Nasser Hospital said. Israel's military said it was not aware of a strike in Khan Younis. Two separate Israeli strikes killed one person each in Gaza City on Friday, according to health officials at Shifa hospital. Israel's military confirmed it struck two separate areas in the city, without elaborating. The five deaths are the latest in Gaza since an October ceasefire deal attempted to halt a more than two-year war between Israel and Hamas. While the heaviest fighting has subsided, Israeli forces have carried out repeated airstrikes, killing at least 1,303 Palestinians, according to health officials in Gaza. Thousands of sailors stranded by Iran war The UN's maritime agency said Friday that 19 seafarers have been killed and at least 6,000 remain stranded on hundreds of ships unable to leave the region since the start of the Iran war on February 28. There have been at least 70 attacks on international shipping in the Persian Gulf, according to the International Maritime Organisation. IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez urged practical solutions and renewed cooperation to restore freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. About 20 per cent of the world's traded oil and natural gas passed through the vital commercial waterway at the mouth of the Persian Gulf before the war. Iran and Russia look to revive energy deal Iran's ambassador to Russia on Friday said the two countries are seeking to deepen links between their energy grids by reviving a plan that dates to 2022, according to Iranian state media. Umud Shokri, a fellow at George Mason University, said the plan calls for piping 55 billion cubic metres of Russian gas annually into Iran, via Azerbaijan. He said that would help Iran weather US economic pressure by alleviating seasonal shortages of gas, though there are significant hurdles, as building out the infrastructure would be expensive and time-consuming. “It is more than bluster, but not yet a game changer,” Shokri said. US imposes restrictions on Egyptian bank The Trump administration is taking steps to limit an Egyptian bank's operations in the United Arab Emirates. Banque Misr, Egypt's second-largest bank, is accused of serving as an economic lifeline to Iran's leadership. But under a new rule proposed by the US Treasury, the bank's Emirati branches would be severed from access to the US financial system. Iran objects to US economic pressure Iran's Foreign Ministry on Friday condemned a new round of US economic measures against the country, calling them “economic terrorism” and saying Tehran would use all available means to counter them. The ministry said the sanctions violated international law and called on other countries to refrain from implementing them. It accused Washington of using the US dollar to pressure other countries into complying with its policies. Earlier this week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowed to fully sever Iran from the global economy and threatened countries that continue to do business with Iran with secondary sanctions. It was part of the US campaign to use economic pressure to try and wring concessions from Iran. Finland to stop providing UN agency aid for Palestine Finland said it will not extend an agreement to provide humanitarian aid with the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, or UNRWA. Israel's Foreign Ministry, which has accused the UN agency of being a “hotbed of terrorism,” welcomed the news. UNRWA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Finland provided UNRWA with 5 million euros (USD 5.8 million) annually under a multi-year deal set to expire later this year. Ville Tavio, the country's foreign trade minister, said in a post on X that aid to Palestinian territories would instead be provided through other channels, such as the UN's World Food Programme. UK warns Israel against removing British officials The United Kingdom warned against any attempt by Israel to remove British officials from the Gaza ceasefire coordination centre on Friday, after reports that Israel was considering expelling UK officials. The UK government said any move to remove its officials would “undermine shared efforts” to implement the 20-point Gaza peace plan. The comments came in response to reports that Israel is considering expelling officials from Britain and other European nations from the monitoring centre. Israel has already removed two Dutch diplomats from the ceasefire centre. The country said Thursday that the decision was in response to a Dutch ban on the trade of Israeli products from the occupied West Bank and other “anti-Israel measures.”

stories.headline: Nepal GLOF tragedy puts spotlight on Kashmir’s lagging preparedness
stories.title: Nepal GLOF tragedy puts spotlight on Kashmir’s lagging preparedness
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 28: The recent glacial lake outburst flood in Nepal has sharpened focus on vulnerabilities at home. There is a chasm in J&K, between the on-ground preparedness here, compared with other Himalayan states. Five glacial lakes in the Kashmir Himalayas, the Bramsar, Chirsar, Nundkol, Gangabal and Bhagsar, have been classified as having “very high susceptibility” to Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). This was revealed by a study by Department of Geoinformatics, University of Kashmir, published in the Journal of Glaciology. The lakes, as per the study, threaten roughly 2704 buildings, about 15 major bridges, stretches of road and one hydropower plant in Ganderbal, Shopian, and Kulgam districts. Associate Professor at Department of Geoinfomatics, University of Kashmir, Irfan Rashid, said the lakes are not "unstable" at present, but nevertheless "risky". "In a few years, the lakes like Gangabal may be a risk. Gangabal has Harmukh glacier upstream, and it is on a steep slope. In view of disaster like that of Nepal, we must take into account such factors as well," he said. In addition, Rashid said, glacial-lake volume assessment could help in improving data that Government must take into consideration. "Our urban planning and disaster mitigation policies need to take into account the environment and geological research carried out by academia here," he said. Rashid said that Chirsar and Bramsar, two glacial lakes in Kulgam district have an ice-contacts - lakes have formed at the terminal point of the glacier. Among lakes in Kashmir, these have the highest susceptibility to GLOF, he said. Earlier this year, a reply to a starred question in the Legislative Assembly had the government acknowledging the findings. The government outlined a roadmap that included continuous remote-sensing and field monitoring, installation of early-warning systems, bathymetric surveys planned for 2026, development of ecozonation plans, and integration of GLOF scenarios into district disaster plans. The work on mountain-specific early-warning prototypes that combine satellite data, field observations and real-time sensors is already underway at University of Kashmir. However, these measures have largely remained on paper only. Many Himalyan states have made progress. Sikkim now has operational water-level sensors, automatic weather stations and India’s first dedicated GLOF early-warning system. This followed the 2023 South Lhonak disaster. Himachal Pradesh has a C-DAC prototype which has been tested at Sissu and is being scaled up. J&K has no real-time monitoring hardware or functional early-warning network. Bathymetric surveys needed for accurate flood modelling are a far call. Dr Rashid said risk mitigation in Himalayas will require study of thousands of lakes. This, he said, is a serious and long-term exercise. The national GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme has initially prioritised Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh. Kashmir and Ladakh were added later. While the scientific baseline in Kashmir has a solid scientific strength, the absence of installed sensors, operational alerts and completed field assessments leaves it lagging. This is crucial as climate-driven glacial risks are rising across the Himalayan range.

stories.headline: Lawyers must re-enter political mainstream
stories.title: Lawyers must re-enter political mainstream
stories.summary: India’s democratic journey has always been closely intertwined with the legal profession. From the struggle for independence to the making of the Constitution and the establishment of parliamentary democracy, lawyers played an extraordinary role in shaping the nation. The freedom movement was not merely a political struggle; it was also a struggle for civil liberties, equality, dignity and the rule of law. Mahatma Gandhi, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Dr. Rajendra Prasad and countless other lawyers stepped beyond their courtrooms to stand with the people and lead the country towards freedom. The composition of the first Parliament of independent India reflected this remarkable tradition. Around 70 lawyers were members of the first Lok Sabha. Their presence was not accidental. They understood that political freedom would have little meaning unless it was translated into constitutional governance, social justice, economic opportunity and protection of individual rights. Their legal training enabled them to participate meaningfully in framing laws, scrutinising executive action and building the institutional architecture of the Republic. It is worth asking why this tradition has weakened over the years. Lawyers continue to occupy a position of considerable respect in courts and public discourse, and many distinguished members of the profession continue to serve in Parliament and State legislatures. Yet, in relative terms, the participation of lawyers in electoral politics and public life has declined. This should concern everyone committed to the health of Indian democracy. When lawyers withdraw from public life, politics loses an important source of constitutional knowledge, institutional experience and principled accountability. The courtroom and the political arena are different, but they are not disconnected. A lawyer appearing before a constitutional court may argue about fundamental rights, federalism, separation of powers or administrative accountability. A legislator must confront these very principles while making laws and scrutinising government. Lawyers understand how an apparently simple administrative decision can affect the liberty, livelihood, property or dignity of an ordinary citizen. This experience can make an important contribution to public policy. Lawyers are also professionally trained to question power. Legal practice requires examining facts, testing evidence, identifying contradictions and demanding reasons for the exercise of authority. In a democracy, these qualities are indispensable. Political power must remain accountable; legislation must be carefully scrutinised; executive authority must remain within constitutional limits; and institutions must function according to law. Lawyers are therefore naturally equipped to ask a fundamental democratic question: Is this exercise of power lawful, fair and constitutionally justified? At the same time, legal training alone does not make someone a good politician or administrator. Politics requires empathy, patience, social understanding, organisational ability, communication, political judgment and moral courage. A lawyer entering politics must understand the lives of people beyond the courtroom—the farmer facing agrarian distress, the worker seeking employment, the student struggling for opportunity, the displaced family seeking rehabilitation and the young person searching for a secure future. That is precisely why more lawyers should enter public life. Their purpose should not be to create a separate class of legal politicians, but to bring constitutional consciousness into the political process. They can help bridge the gap between constitutional promises and everyday realities. They can explain complex questions of law and policy in language ordinary citizens understand, challenge misinformation and insist that political programmes remain consistent with constitutional values. Justice, after all, is not confined to courtrooms. Poverty, unemployment, discrimination, displacement, custodial violence, unequal access to education and healthcare, environmental degradation and denial of basic services are also questions of justice. Courts can provide remedies in individual cases, but many structural problems require legislative and political solutions. Laws have to be enacted, budgets allocated, institutions strengthened and policies implemented. Lawyers who understand both the law and the lived experience of citizens can therefore make a significant contribution to translating constitutional ideals into effective governance. This responsibility becomes even more important as India’s young population becomes increasingly politically conscious. Gen Z is not merely an audience of politics; it is increasingly becoming a participant in it. Young Indians are entering public debate with new expectations of transparency, accountability, employment, quality education and dignity. They are also confronting questions relating to climate change, technology, artificial intelligence, privacy, data protection, surveillance and freedom of expression in the digital age. The legal fraternity must engage with this generation—not merely as teachers, but as listeners and partners. Gen Z is bringing new forms of political participation and communication. Lawyers must understand these changes and help ensure that technological and social transformation takes place within the framework of constitutional rights and human dignity. Artificial intelligence and digital technologies, for example, raise profound questions about privacy, employment, intellectual property, discrimination, surveillance and accountability. Social media has transformed political communication while creating new challenges involving misinformation and freedom of expression. These are not distant legal questions. They will directly influence the future of Indian democracy. Lawyers with a sound understanding of constitutional principles have an important role in ensuring that technological progress does not come at the cost of fundamental freedoms. Lawyers can also bring greater seriousness and evidence-based reasoning to political debate. Their professional experience encourages them to distinguish fact from allegation and argument from evidence. But legal expertise must never become a means of hiding moral responsibility behind technicalities. Constitutionalism is not merely about procedures and institutional boundaries. At its heart are human dignity, liberty, equality and justice. Political parties and the Bar also have responsibilities. Opportunities should be created for younger members of the Bar to participate in policy discussions, legislative research and public affairs. article_sentences: The Supreme Court recently refused to entertain a petition challenging the 2026 amendments to the Mizo Marriage, Divorce and Inheritance of Property Act, 2014, which are stated to be discriminatory towards Mizo women who marry non-Mizo men.
A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana observed that the issue could be effectively addressed by the jurisdictional High Court.

Considering however the petitioner's apprehension that the matter may not be heard at the Aizawl Bench, due to a charged atmosphere, the Court gave her liberty to approach the Principal bench of the Guwahati High Court.
It was opined that the matter prima facie requires preferential attention.
Briefly put, the petition challenged amendments made to Sections 2, 3(m), 25 and 26(1) of The Mizo Marriage, Divorce and Inheritance of Property Act, 2014.
According to the plea, the amended Section 2 restricts the applicability of the Act to marriages where both spouses are Mizo or where only the husband is Mizo.
Consequently, a Mizo woman marrying a non-Mizo man is excluded from the statutory framework, while a Mizo man continues to remain covered irrespective of the identity of his spouse.
Further, the petitioner contended that the amendment to Section 3(m), which redefines the expression 'Mizo', was made to give significance to paternal lineage and the identity of the spouse.
Earlier, the Act applied to any person belonging to a Mizo tribe and extended to marriage where the male member belonged to a Mizo tribe.
Now, the amendment requires both parties to be Mizo or applies to male members belonging to the Mizo tribe.
It was highlighted that the earlier definition of 'Mizo' included persons by birth, adoption, and those accepted by the community.
But now, it only includes those individuals by birth or those whose father belongs to a Mizo tribe, thereby introducing a strictly patrilineal standard.

stories.headline: Changing Lifelines – Part 3 : Kashmir’s rivers brace for uneven, extreme future as climate shifts hydrological patterns
stories.title: Changing Lifelines – Part 3 : Kashmir’s rivers brace for uneven, extreme future as climate shifts hydrological patterns
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 28: Kashmir’s rivers, including the main lifeline – Jhelum, could be heading towards a more uneven and extreme future as climate change reshapes the Valley’s temperature, precipitation and hydrological patterns, according to a study published in the international journal Discover Applied Sciences. The study states that Kashmir’s rivers are bracing for a wild new water cycle by 2100. The research employs the Soil and Water Integrated Model (SWIM), a GIS-based hydrological modelling system that links climate and land-use changes with hydrology, vegetation and water quality. Researchers used observed discharge data alongside multiple climate projections to examine how Kashmir’s hydrological behaviour could evolve over the course of the 21st century. The assessment compares the historical period of 1985–2014 with three future periods—2016–2043, 2044–2071 and 2072–2100—under three greenhouse-gas emission pathways: SSP1-2.6, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5. Five Earth System Models—GFDL-ESM4, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, MRI-ESM2-0 and UKESM1-0-LL—were incorporated to capture a range of possible climate futures. To understand seasonal changes in river behaviour, the researchers divided the hydrological year into three phases--snow accumulation from October to February, snowmelt from March to June, and the monsoon season from July to September. “By 2100, the water cycle of Kashmir rivers, especially river jehlum will turn more wild,” the study reads. The study goes beyond simply examining whether rainfall or temperature will rise or fall. It also investigates how water will be distributed through the year, an important question for a region where rivers depend on the delicate interplay of snowfall, snowmelt, rainfall and runoff. Researchers used the Gini coefficient to assess changes in the distribution of annual streamflow. In hydrological terms, a higher Gini coefficient indicates that a greater share of annual river discharge is concentrated within fewer days, pointing towards less evenly distributed flows. A value approaching one would indicate extreme concentration, while zero would represent perfectly uniform distribution. They also examined the emergence of climate signals—the point at which changes in temperature, precipitation or river discharge become sufficiently distinct from the historical baseline to be detected. Using a 31-year running mean, the study considered a climate signal to have emerged when it moved beyond the historical baseline mean by more than one standard deviation. For Kashmir’s flood-prone Himalayan catchments, the study’s assessment of extreme flows is particularly significant. Researchers employed the Gumbel distribution, a statistical approach commonly used to analyse extreme hydrological events, to examine changes in flood levels. “Annual maximum river discharges were fitted to the Gumbel distribution and changes in 30-year flood levels were estimated, offering an indication of how climate change could alter the magnitude of rare but potentially destructive floods,” the study reads. “The SWIM model was calibrated and validated using observed discharge data from 1994 to 2004. Its performance was assessed through several indicators, including the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), coefficient of determination (R²), Percent Bias (PBIAS), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Volumetric Efficiency and Mean Error. ” The researchers note that, for daily flows, watershed-scale modelling is generally considered satisfactory when R² exceeds 0.60, NSE exceeds 0.50 and PBIAS remains within ±15 per cent. The study highlights a crucial dimension of Kashmir’s climate challenge--the question may no longer be simply whether the Valley receives more or less water, but when that water arrives, how quickly it moves through the river system and how unevenly it is distributed. “For Kashmir, where communities, agriculture, hydropower and ecosystems remain closely tied to river systems, changing flow regimes could have far-reaching consequences. A greater concentration of water during shorter periods could increase pressure on flood-management systems, while altered seasonal flows could affect water availability during other parts of the year,” according to the research. The findings reinforce the need for climate-resilient water planning across the Himalayan region, with greater emphasis on seasonal changes, flow variability and extreme events rather than relying solely on historical hydrological patterns. As Kashmir’s weather becomes increasingly erratic, the study offers a compelling warning: the Valley’s future water crisis may not be about having too little or too much water—it may be about water arriving at the wrong time, in the wrong place and with greater force.

stories.headline: Defence Ministry eases export rules to boost defence exports
stories.title: Defence Ministry eases export rules to boost defence exports
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 28: The Ministry of Defence has introduced a series of reforms to simplify procedures for defence exports and make it easier for Indian manufacturers to access international markets. The reforms, undertaken by the Department of Defence Production under the guidance of Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, aim to reduce procedural requirements while ensuring that national security safeguards remain in place. Under the revised Defence Export Standard Operating Procedure (SOP), stakeholder consultation will no longer be required for exports of non-lethal defence items to most destinations, except sensitive countries. The requirement has also been removed for exports of all items for international tenders and exhibitions, allowing Indian companies to pursue overseas opportunities more quickly. The Ministry has also substantially revised the Open General Export Licence (OGEL) framework. The OGEL is a standing export authorisation that allows eligible companies to undertake multiple consignments of specified defence items without obtaining a separate licence for each shipment. Three existing OGEL SOPs covering major platforms and equipment, parts and components, and intra-company transfer of technology have been merged into a single unified SOP. The validity of OGEL has also been increased from two to three years, reducing the need for frequent renewals. The countries covered under OGEL have been expanded from 41 to all countries, barring specified sensitive or restricted nations and countries facing UN Security Council sanctions or arms embargoes. A new provision will also facilitate Indian companies that have long-term contracts with foreign original equipment manufacturers. In eligible cases, OGEL validity can be aligned with the duration of the underlying contract, subject to prescribed conditions. The range of items eligible for OGEL has also been expanded. The revised framework permits civil-end-use exports of specified parts and components of small-calibre arms and protective equipment. The government said the reforms would particularly benefit Indian defence manufacturers, including MSMEs, by reducing repetitive approvals and enabling them to respond faster to international tenders and exhibitions. The government said the changes are aimed at further strengthening India’s position as a reliable and competitive global defence manufacturing and export partner, in line with the objectives of Make in India and Aatmanirbhar Bharat.

article_sentences: SEBI on Friday barred Debock Industries Ltd and its managing director Mukesh Singh for seven years and ordered disgorgement of unlawful gains totalling ₹59.30 crore from multiple individuals in a case involving an alleged accounting fraud.
Also, other entities have been barred from the securities market for periods ranging from three to five years, according to SEBI's final order.
The markets regulator has also directed Debock Industries to bring back ₹49 crore diverted from its 2023 rights issue, along with applicable interest.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has also slapped penalties totalling more than ₹29 crore on the company, Singh and others.
Singh alone has been fined ₹20.10 crore.

Summing up the alleged scheme, SEBI in its 121-page final order said Debock Industries, with Singh at the helm, inflated its financials through fictitious sales and purchases and circular transactions after its listing on NSE Emerge.

“Noticee No. 1 (Debock Industries) with Noticee No. 2 (Singh) at the helm of its affairs, post its listing on NSE Emerge, inflated its financials through fictitious sales and purchases and circular transactions.
The inflation of financials allowed Noticee No. 1 to migrate to the main board of NSE,” SEBI said.
“On the main board, Noticee No.1 (Debock Industries) came up with fraudulent issuance of preferential allotments, bonus issue and rights issue, and increased its capital base,” it said.
Later, around 4.21 crore shares worth ₹59.30 crore obtained through fraudulent preferential issue and bonus issue were dumped on gullible investors.
“The fraudulent scheme was masterminded by Noticee No. 2 (Singh) with aid and assistance of Noticee No. 3 (Sunil Kalot), 4 (Priyanka Sharma) and 27 (Gaurav Jain),” SEBI added.
The regulator quantified the unlawful gains at ₹59.30 crore.
